newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - Easing in RBNZ policy will be short-lived.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Easing in RBNZ policy will be short-lived.

text.p: By Bevan Graham, Chief Economist, Westpac NZ.
WELLINGTON, Nov 15 - As I put pen to paper (finger to keyboard) we are no closer to an election outcome.

But while the politicians negotiate, the economics continue to roll on. Given I believe there is nothing worse than an economist prognosticating over politics, I think I'll play it safe and stick to what I know best.

What has sparked most interest in the market post-election was the release of September quarter inflation data showing a far better outcome than the market and (more importantly) the Reserve Bank were expecting, with underlying inflation rising just 0.3 percent for an annual rate of 2.3 percent.
Not only was the overall result a good number, the make-up of the result couldn't have been better.

The housing group still provided the most significant increase for the quarter, but at 0.6 percent, this was well below recent levels. Price falls in this category were just where we wanted to see them - construction expenses and maintenance materials.

This result represents the first evidence that the slowdown in the rate of growth in activity is leading to an easing in price pressures. This has confirmed our view that the Reserve Bank will allow some easing in the December Monetary Policy Statement.
However, there are a number of question marks around how the economy is likely to perform during 1997 which, on balance, suggests to us that any easing will be short lived.
Firstly, recent increases in medical insurance premiums and petrol prices have not yet been captured in the figures and "core" food prices are still rising strongly.

Secondly, we still have a concern that we don't know to what extent the slowdown in activity prior to the election was due to high interest rates or election uncertainty. Once the election uncertainty is out of the way we will be watching for any significant rebounding activity in the residential property market in particular.
Household behaviour has continued to vex policy makers (and economists) who had hoped to see higher interest rates dim demand. Instead lending to households continues on at double digit growth.

On top of this the Westpac McDermott Miller Consumer Confidence Index rose to 121.2 in the September quarter after falling to 113.1 in March -- back into solidly optimistic territory. All the hallmarks of a strong pick-up in activity once the election uncertainty is out of the way.

But one inflation risk factor that we can start to feel a little more comfortable about now is the potential increase in activity after the first round of the tax cuts. Retail sales fell a seasonally adjusted 0.6 percent in August. This result followed a 3.2 percent fall in June and a 2.3 percent rise in July. The annual rate of growth has slipped from 4.2 percent in July to 2.3 percent in August.
This confirms the view that we have held for a long time -- that monetary conditions are sufficiently tight to offset any stimulatory impact from the tax cuts.

It also fits in with anecdotal evidence telling us that there was a pick-up in retail sales immediately after the tax cuts in July, but that subsequent months have been pretty flat. The third factor we need to consider is the labour market and its reluctance to adjust to the lower growth path.

Over the past year employment growth has not slowed to the same extent as overall growth in activity, suggesting an erosion of labour productivity -- although latest labour market data suggests that at least productivity growth is now less negative than before.
But combine this erosion in labour productivity with continued increases in wages and we have a picture of rising unit labour costs.
This has been of considerable concern to the Reserve Bank given the close relationship between unit labour costs and underlying inflation.
The problem has been that firms have been reluctant to let labour go during the slowdown because of the problems they had getting labour in the first place given the skills shortage.

But this was only ever going to be a temporary problem before either growth picked up or firms eventually let the labour go. We believe the Reserve Bank will be reluctant to see conditions ease too significantly without seeing signs of reduced pressure on unit labour costs.

If we factor in our expectations of the annual rate of wage increase reaching 3.5 percent in the year to August when the Quarterly Employment Survey is released next week, we will see the annual rate of increase in unit labour costs (our own measure -- not an official statistic) remain at 4.6 percent. This will be the first stabilisation in the rate of increase since the beginning of 1994 - just what the Reserve Bank needs to see.

The final factor that would make the Reserve Bank a little anxious about any significant easing at this stage is the still uncertain political outlook (sorry, politics had to get a mention at some stage). And with an uncertain political outlook comes uncertainty about the outlook for fiscal policy.

The Reserve Bank has already factored in a further easing in fiscal policy for fiscal 1997/98 in the form of increased expenditure and the second tranche of the National Government's tax cuts -- all of which have been flagged for some time.
However there is still considerable uncertainty about to what extent fiscal policy may be eased further, and in what form that easing may take.
Whatever the outcome of the election, it is likely that fiscal policy will be easier in 1997/98 than what we have been assuming under a no policy change scenario.
So what does all of this mean for monetary policy? We continue to expect there will be scope for lower interest rates towards the end of this year and in the first part of 1997.

However, given expectations of looser fiscal policy and the likely resurgence in domestic demand as a result of the easing in monetary conditions, we expect a move back to tighter conditions towards the end of 1997.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
